newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bruton sees some progress on EU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Bruton sees some progress on EU budget pact.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Tuesday that President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had made some progress towards resolving a dispute over a European Union budget discipline pact but that the issue was not yet settled.
He was speaking to reporters after meeting Chirac a day after the French president and Kohl met at a summit in Nuremberg, Germany.
"The president and the chancellor did make some progress on the matter but it is not resolved yet," he told a news conference.
Germany continued to insist that there should be numerical definitions of the kinds of exceptional circumstances which would exempt a member state from fines under the pact, he said.

"The position of other member states is that they agree there should be figures which define what is exceptional for the purpose of not having a fine. They agree those figures should be taken into account...but they don't want it to be absolutely automatic. They want a margin for appreciation," he said.
"The solution lies in defining or constraining the margin for appreciation," Bruton said.
For example, one could limit the margin for appreciation to the level of the (EU) council of ministers rather than extending it to the European Commission, he said.
"It all hinges on assurances that the exceptional circumstances exception will not be used in a politically easy way," he said.
Bruton noted that the Maastricht treaty already allowed a margin for judgement on deficit overshoots.
It was possible, however, that a political declaration could be made to accompany the treaty on budget discipline.
"I hope the finance ministers will be able to give us the text of a political declaration," he said.
Finance ministers are due to meet in Dublin on Thursday evening ahead of a summit of EU leaders on Friday and Saturday.
"Nobody is disagreeing with figures being in the declaration," Bruton said.

He said talks were revolving around whether to define exceptional circumstances as a decline in gross domestic product of 1.5 percent over the year and/or four consecutive quarters of recession. There were discussions as to whether both of these conditions should be met, or one or the other, he said.
"We are seeing a position where people are coming closer together," he said. But he added, "they all still have their starting positions on the table."
He said he could not say whether any political declaration on fiscal discipline would make a specific reference to the need for a strong currency.
He also noted that there was no deadline for agreement on the budget stability pact.
"There are strong arguments for completing this business before the Dublin summit...but if we don't, there is no deadline," he said.
